query: Consider the following context: High-entropy alloy (HEA) multilayers represent a promising class of advanced coating materials due to their superior mechanical properties, corrosion resistance, and irradiation tolerance. However, the specific role of interface coherency on the creep behavior of HEA multilayers remains unclear. In that context, which material can be used for transition between diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated creep mechanisms, and why?

generation.hypothesis: In HEA multilayers, incorporating a thin, coherent interlayer of a eutectic high-entropy alloy based on the AlCoCrFeNi system can serve as a transition material that moderates the shift from diffusion‐mediated to dislocation‐mediated creep. The coherent interlayer is expected to suppress excessive atomic diffusion at lower temperatures while still permitting diffusional accommodation at high temperatures, thereby facilitating a gradual change in the dominant creep mechanism.
generation.material_initial_state: HEA multilayers with standard (possibly semi-coherent or incoherent) interfaces between layers that primarily exhibit diffusion‐mediated creep at high homologous temperatures.
generation.intervention: Introduce a thin interlayer composed of an AlCoCrFeNi-based eutectic high-entropy alloy between the primary HEA layers, engineered to maintain high interface coherency with adjacent layers.
generation.conditions: Creep testing performed over a temperature range that spans the regime where diffusion-mediated creep dominates (high temperatures) to where dislocation-mediated creep becomes more pronounced (lower temperatures). Other conditions (stress, layer thickness) remain consistent between control and modified samples.
generation.structural_mediator: A coherently bonded, ultra-thin interlayer that acts as a structural bridge between HEA layers, maintaining lattice continuity and reducing local diffusivity at the interfaces.
generation.mechanism: The coherent interlayer is designed to reduce the effective diffusion paths at the interface by matching lattice parameters, thus lowering the propensity for vacancy diffusion and diffusion creep at lower temperatures. Conversely, at higher temperatures the interlayer still allows sufficient atomic mobility for diffusion creep but also facilitates dislocation nucleation by offering reduced barriers for dislocation motion as interface coherency is maintained.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to HEA multilayers without the interlayer, samples with the AlCoCrFeNi-based interlayer should exhibit a measurable reduction in overall creep rate at lower temperatures due to enhanced dislocation activity, along with a distinct change in the activation energy for creep, indicating a mechanism transition from diffusional to dislocation-mediated behavior.
generation.baseline: HEA multilayers lacking the engineered interlayer, which are expected to retain higher diffusion-dominated creep rates across the same temperature range.
generation.boundary: This transition effect is expected only when the interlayer is thin enough to preserve coherency and when processing conditions avoid the formation of secondary phases at the interface. At extreme temperatures or with significant interlayer thickness deviations, the mechanism transition might not be as distinct.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal composition and thickness of the AlCoCrFeNi-based interlayer necessary to yield the desired coherent interface and the precise temperature range over which the transition occurs are currently uncertain and require experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of HEA multilayer samples: one set with a thin, coherent AlCoCrFeNi-based eutectic interlayer inserted between each HEA layer, and a control set without the interlayer. Subject both sets to creep tests over a temperature range (e.g., from moderately high temperatures where diffusion creep dominates to lower temperatures where dislocation creep should prevail). Use transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and diffraction techniques to assess the interface coherency and identify the active deformation mechanisms. Compare the creep rates and activation energies between the two sets.
measurements: Creep strain rate as a function of temperature
Activation energy for creep via Arrhenius analysis
Dislocation density and activity observed via TEM
Interface coherency and phase structure via diffraction/XRD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the insertion of the AlCoCrFeNi-based interlayer does not lead to a statistically significant change in the creep behavior (i.e., no noticeable shift from diffusion-mediated to dislocation-mediated mechanisms as evidenced by similar creep rates, activation energies, and dislocation structures compared to the control), or if the interlayer fails to maintain coherent interfaces, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Dual-phase high entropy alloys have recently attracted widespread attention as advanced structural materials due to their unique microstructure, excellent mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance. However, their molten salt corrosion behavior has not been reported, which is critical in evaluating their application merit in the areas of concentrating solar power and nuclear energy. Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205. Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205. There was selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205. This was attributed to micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in each alloy that was measured in terms of Volta potential difference using a scanning kelvin probe.
